q: Le Chatelier's principle was discovered by French Chemist Henri Louis Le Chatelier in 1884.
e: The text states this historical fact regarding the discovery of the principle.

q: If a system is in equilibrium and when any of the factors affecting the chemical equilibrium is changed, the equilibrium shifts so as to enhance the effect of the change.
e: The equilibrium shifts so as to cancel out the effect of the change, not enhance it.

q: Once equilibrium is established in a system, no further change is apparent as long as the external factors remain unchanged.
e: A system at equilibrium remains unchanged if external factors are constant.

q: The changes in concentration, temperature, and pressure of the system are external factors that affect equilibrium.
e: These three factors are identified as the stresses that affect equilibrium.

q: In some cases, stress causes no shift in the equilibrium, especially when the moles of reactants and products are equal after the change in the pressure of gases.
e: Pressure changes do not shift equilibrium if the number of moles of gas is the same on both sides.

q: Le Chatelier's principle describes how a chemical equilibrium shifts in response to a stress within an open system.
e: Le Chatelier's principle applies to shifts in response to stress within an enclosed or closed system.

q: A change in concentration, temperature, or pressure makes a difference in the amount of product formed in a reaction.
e: These factors alter the equilibrium position and thus the amount of product formed.

q: A catalyst does not affect the equilibrium concentrations and there is no change in equilibrium.
e: Catalysts speed up the rate of reaching equilibrium but do not shift the equilibrium position.

q: Adding or removing a reactant or product from a reaction mixture at equilibrium will always disturb the equilibrium.
e: Changing the concentration of any reactant or product disturbs the equilibrium state.

q: When the concentration of a reactant is increased, the system responds by proceeding in the reverse direction in favour of reactants.
e: The system responds by proceeding in the forward direction in favour of products to remove the added reactant.

q: When the concentration of a reactant is decreased, the system responds by adding the concentration of the reactant, thus the reaction proceeds in the reverse direction.
e: The reverse reaction is favoured to replace the removed reactant.

q: When the concentration of a product is increased, the system responds by removing the concentration of the product, thus the reaction proceeds in the forward direction.
e: The reaction proceeds in the reverse direction in favour of reactants to remove the added product.

q: When the concentration of a product is decreased, the system responds by adding the concentration of the product, thus the reaction proceeds in the forward direction.
e: The forward reaction is favoured to replace the removed product.

q: The effect of temperature on chemical equilibrium depends upon the heat changes ($\Delta H$) of the reaction.
e: Whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic determines the temperature effect.

q: If a thermochemical equation is given, the value of heat change is for the reverse reaction.
e: The value of heat change given in a thermochemical equation is for the forward reaction.

q: A temperature decrease favours an exothermic reaction, and a temperature increase favours an endothermic reaction.
e: This is the fundamental rule for temperature changes according to Le Chatelier's principle.

q: In the case of exothermic reactions, decreasing the temperature favours the exothermic reaction by releasing heat.
e: The system shifts to release heat to counteract the temperature decrease.

q: In the case of endothermic reactions, increasing the temperature shifts the equilibrium towards the reverse reaction.
e: Increasing the temperature favours the endothermic forward reaction by absorbing heat.

q: The decomposition of $N_2O_4$ to $NO_2$ has a positive $\Delta H$, which means that the forward reaction is exothermic.
e: A positive $\Delta H$ means the forward reaction is endothermic.

q: When the temperature of the $N_2O_4$ and $NO_2$ equilibrium mixture is decreased, it favours the exothermic reaction and more $N_2O_4$ is obtained.
e: Decreasing temperature shifts the equilibrium to the left, forming more colourless $N_2O_4$.

q: Pressure changes markedly affect the solid or liquid phases in a chemical equilibrium.
e: Pressure changes do not markedly affect solid or liquid phases; they primarily affect the gas phase.

q: The pressure of a gas mixture at a given temperature is determined by the number of gas molecules in a given volume.
e: This is the physical basis for why pressure affects gaseous equilibria.

q: If the pressure is increased, the position of equilibrium will shift towards the side with more moles of gas.
e: Increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas.

q: According to Le Chatelier's principle, as pressure decreases, the equilibrium moves toward the side of the reaction with more moles of gas.
e: Decreasing pressure favours the side that produces more gas molecules to restore pressure.

q: If the number of moles of gas is the same on both sides of the reversible chemical equation, increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right.
e: If the moles of gas are equal, changing the pressure has no effect on the equilibrium position.

q: The synthesis of ammonia (Haber process) is a good example of an industrial process that uses Le Chatelier's principle.
e: The Haber process conditions are specifically chosen based on Le Chatelier's principle.

q: In the synthesis of ammonia, the forward reaction is favoured at high temperatures because the reaction is exothermic.
e: The forward reaction is favoured at low temperatures because it is exothermic.

q: The forward reaction in ammonia production is favoured by high pressure because there are four moles of reactants for every two moles of product formed.
e: High pressure shifts the equilibrium to the side with fewer moles of gas (the product side).

q: The catalyst used in the Haber process is iron(III) oxide with a small amount of aluminium oxide.
e: This is the specific catalyst mixture mentioned for ammonia production.

q: The catalyst used in the Haber process will speed up the production and this has helped reduce the energy requirements.
e: Catalysts lower the activation energy, reducing the energy needed for the industrial process.

q: Methanol is an alcohol that is used in fuels, making methyl esters, and creating urea-formaldehyde resin glues through the oxidation of methanol.
e: These are the industrial uses of methanol listed in the textbook.

q: Methanol is produced from carbon monoxide and hydrogen in an endothermic reaction.
e: The production of methanol from carbon monoxide and hydrogen is an exothermic reaction ($\Delta H = -$).

q: To produce the maximum yield of methanol, the position of equilibrium must be shifted to the right by decreasing the temperature.
e: Since the forward reaction is exothermic, decreasing the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right.

q: The production of methanol is carried out at a temperature of 250 °C using the catalyst Cu-ZnO-Al2O3.
e: These are the specific industrial conditions and catalyst stated for methanol production.

q: According to Le Chatelier's principle, increasing the pressure will shift the equilibrium to form fewer moles of methanol.
e: Increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium to form more moles of methanol (the side with fewer gas moles).
